coach_says: Taking with the b-pawn puts your own pawn in front of your a8 rook and opens the b-file for White: Rb1 and Rb7 hits c7 and your rooks are stuck defending. First play c6 to kick the rook off d5, then take on a5 with the rook, which then goes on to attack a4 and c4. When you recapture, ask which recapture makes your rook active and which hands your opponent an open file.
concept: opened a file for their rook

coach_says: Your queen on f3 takes away the g5 knight's best retreat square. After ...h6 the knight has nowhere good to go (Nh3 runs into ...d5 and ...Nd4 hitting your queen), so you end up giving knight and bishop for rook and pawn on f7. f7 is guarded by the castled rook, so it is not a target any more; develop with Nc3, c3 or a4 and bring the knight back to f3 instead.

Recapture with the knight, not the bishop. After Bxd5 Nxd5 Nxd5, White hits your queen with Bg5 and then goes after your knights on d5 and c6 with Be4 or Bb5, while your king is still in the centre. With Nxd5 Nxd5 Bxd5 your bishop on d5 stays and eyes f3, so Bg5 can be met by ...Bxf3. Before recapturing, picture which of your pieces will be left standing on that square and whether it can be chased.

You are a pawn up, but your king is still on e1 and only one minor piece is out. f4 spends a move on a pawn and lets Black take on a1 first, so Bxa1 puts your bishop in the corner and ...Qa8 attacks it, while ...exf4 starts opening lines towards your king. Trading rooks yourself with Rxa8 and then developing with Ne2, d3 and castling keeps your extra pawn safe.
also: trade on the open file first

coach_says: When your bishop was attacked you retreated, but dxe5 was stronger because it opens the d-file: your queen on d2 then attacks the knight on d5, which nothing defends. If Black takes your bishop with ...gxh4, you take the knight with Qxd5. After Bg3 Black plays ...e4, kicking your knight and gaining space. When a piece is attacked, look for a counter-threat before you retreat.
also: open the file onto a loose piece

coach_says: Your bishop on c1 was the only piece guarding b2. After Bf4, ...Qxb2 grabs the pawn and attacks your c3 knight a second time (the d4 bishop already hits it) and also your a1 rook. Be3 was better: it challenges Black's strong bishop on d4, and if ...Qxb2 then Bxd4 wins the bishop. Before moving a piece, check what it was guarding.

When Black puts a pawn on d5 against your e4 pawn, the simple answer is exd5, and after ...Qxd5 you develop Nc3 with a tempo on the queen. f3 develops nothing, takes the f3 square from your knight and weakens the diagonal to your king (e1-h4). In the opening, prefer moves that develop pieces or take in the centre over pawn moves like f3.

White's c4 pawn is protected only by the d3 pawn. If you play dxe4 first and White recaptures dxe4, that pawn has left d3 and your bishop on e6 can take on c4 for free. Bb4 develops, but it lets White play exd5 and attack your centre with d4. When your pawn can take, check whether the recapture pulls away a defender.
concept: pull away the defender of c4
also: resolve the central tension on your terms

coach_says: Your d5 pawn was hanging: the knight on c3 attacks it and your queen cannot help because your own bishop on d7 blocks the d-file. fxe5 does nothing about that, so Nxd5 wins a pawn and the knight lands in the centre near your king. Look for what is undefended before you recapture: ...Bb4 pins the c3 knight so it cannot take, or ...Be6 guards d5.

In the Caro-Kann Advance, f5 is the square your light-squared bishop wants: play ...Bf5 first, then ...e6. Pushing the f-pawn there blocks that bishop in, leaves a hole on e6 and makes your e7 pawn backward. White can then hit your centre with c4 while your pieces are cramped.
c4 is a perfectly good move here, as good as e4 or d4. It grabs space on the queenside and keeps your options open. Carry on developing with d4 or g3 and Nc3.

Good move. White was threatening Bxc6 and Nxe5, winning your e5 pawn, and Nge7 protects the c6 knight so that trick does not work. Next, ...f6 to support e5 and get your king to safety with ...Be6 and ...Kc8 or ...Ke8.
Bb4 pinning the knight is fine and close to the best moves. Keep an eye on Qb3, which attacks b7 now that your bishop has left c8. Then develop with ...Nf6 and castle.

Bc4 is a fine developing move and nearly as good as Nf3 or Nc3. Against the Sicilian, Black can blunt the bishop with ...e6 and then ...d5, gaining a move on it, so be ready to move it again or swap on d5. Carry on with Nf3, Nc3 and castling.

Retreating to e7 is reasonable. Taking on d2 with check was slightly simpler because it doesn't spend time on a bishop that will be pushed around. Either way, castle next and look for ...Nh5 to chase the f4 bishop.

a5 is as good as anything here. You are using your queenside pawns while Black's king is far away. Keep pushing them with your king's support, Kc4 and b4, and don't let the knight pick off g3 for nothing if you can help it.

Qg3+ is the best move. It drives the king back to h1 so that you can take f3 with check next and keep checking while your h-pawn moves up. Keep giving checks that also win pawns, and watch out for perpetual check on your own king.

Kb7 is fine: your king goes to take the a7 pawn, and the a-pawn will then run. You give up f4, but that is fine because Black's king and knight are too far away to stop your a-pawn. Keep the knight near the a-pawn to stop the black knight from blocking it.

Qe7 is a reasonable move in a position that is already a bit worse because of your broken kingside pawns. Get your king to safety, probably on the queenside, and use the open g-file for your rook with ...Rg8.

Excellent. Bb5+ moves the bishop off the d-file, so your queen now attacks the d5 knight. If Black blocks with ...c6, that pawn is pinned to the king and cannot defend d5, so Qxd5 wins a piece. Remember this pattern: a check that also opens a line for another piece.
